title: March Everyone On, or Send Two for Help
actor_role: Captain of the Karluk, in command of the survivors after the sinking
location: Wrangel Island and the sea ice of Long Strait, Chukchi Sea, off the Siberian coast
t0: Mid-to-late March 1914. The Karluk was crushed and sank on January 11; since then Bartlett has led the survivors by relay sledge across weeks of broken, pressure-ridged pack ice -- ridges up to a hundred feet high -- to reach Wrangel Island. Eight of the original twenty-five are already gone: a four-man trailbreaking party sent ahead on January 21, and a separate four who left camp on their own initiative in early February over Bartlett's objection. Neither group has been seen again. No one outside the expedition knows the survivors reached Wrangel Island, or that they are alive at all. Bartlett's stated plan since the sinking has been to take everyone on to the Siberian mainland together. He must now decide whether to do that, or leave the party on the island and make a fast two-man run for help.
context_summary: Your ship is gone, you have walked the survivors across the ice to an island, and eight of your people have already vanished trying to cross ice like this. Nobody in the world knows where you are. You can march everyone onward together, or leave fifteen exhausted people on an island and take the one experienced traveller you have left to go find help.
immediate_outcome: Bartlett left the main party at Wrangel Island and set out for Siberia on March 18, 1914 with Kataktovik, the Inupiat hunter hired at Cape Smythe. The two reached the Siberian coast near Cape Jakan around April 4 after roughly six weeks on moving ice, then travelled overland along the coast before reaching a whaling ship and, eventually, word of the survivors' location reaching rescue authorities.
long_term_outcome: Ice kept the first relief ship, the U.S. Revenue Cutter Bear, from reaching Wrangel Island at all. The schooner King and Winge finally got there on September 7, 1914 -- nearly eight months after the sinking -- and took off the 14 remaining survivors. Three of the party left on the island (Bjarne Mamen, George Malloch and George Breddy) had died during Bartlett's roughly six-month absence. Of the original twenty-five, eleven died. The Anderson trailbreaking party's remains were found on Herald Island a decade later, in 1924; the fate of the four who left in February has never been established. The disaster fed a decades-long dispute between Bartlett and expedition leader Vilhjalmur Stefansson over responsibility for putting the Karluk into the ice in the first place.
uncertainty_factors: Ice and weather on the Siberian side unknown
No way to signal or be found
Whether a relief ship could reach the island at all
Condition of injured members over an open-ended wait

options.label: Lead the whole surviving party onward to Siberia together
options.short_description: Continue the plan announced at the sinking: take all roughly seventeen remaining survivors -- including exhausted and injured members with little Arctic experience -- across the sea ice from Wrangel Island to the Siberian mainland as one body.
options.upside: Keeps the group under its most experienced leader rather than leaving the majority to an indefinite unsupervised wait. More hands for breaking trail, hauling sledges and building shelter. And if the crossing works, everyone reaches safety at once instead of depending on a rescue that someone else must first mount.
options.downside: The party barely survived a shorter crossing of similar ice, and eight men vanished during it. Adding inexperienced, exhausted or injured people to a longer crossing risks losing everyone together if the ice opens or the weather turns -- leaving nobody at all to tell the outside world where they were.
known_tradeoffs: Bartlett had told the men this was the plan when the ship went down, and it avoids abandoning weaker members on a remote island with no certainty that a two-man attempt would succeed or that any relief expedition would ever be sent to a location nobody has reported. versus If the group crossing fails partway -- open water, a storm, exhaustion -- there is no fallback, and everyone who could have raised the alarm is lost at the same time.

options.label: Split the party: two go for help, the rest wait at Wrangel Island
options.short_description: Leave the bulk of the survivors on Wrangel Island, where driftwood and some game are available, while Bartlett and Kataktovik -- the most experienced traveller left -- make a fast, lightly equipped run for the Siberian mainland to raise a rescue.
options.upside: A small, experienced pair moves far faster across shifting ice than a large group carrying its injured. It leaves the weaker survivors somewhere with at least some subsistence rather than force-marching them over more of the same hazard. And it creates a real chance that news of the party's exact location reaches the outside world at all, which at present it cannot.
options.downside: It leaves roughly fifteen people, some already hurt, waiting on a remote island for an open-ended period with limited supplies and no way to communicate, wholly dependent on an attempt whose success is unknown at the moment of departure. If the two die on the ice, nobody will know where to look for the rest.
known_tradeoffs: Most of the ship's company had no meaningful Arctic field experience, and the party had only narrowly survived the shorter crossing; sending the most capable pair gives the best realistic chance of getting anyone out. versus The two-man crossing is itself extraordinarily hazardous -- about six weeks over moving pack ice with no backup -- and those left behind face months of waiting with no guarantee that help, once summoned, can reach them before supplies, health or morale give out.

case_information.content: The Karluk sank on January 11, 1914 after being crushed in pack ice in the Chukchi Sea. The survivors relayed supplies and travelled by stages across broken, pressure-ridged sea ice to reach Wrangel Island.

A four-man advance and trailbreaking party sent out under First Officer Alexander Anderson on January 21, 1914 had not been seen again. Their fate was unknown at this point; their remains were found a decade later, in 1924, on nearby Herald Island.

A separate group of four -- ship's surgeon Alistair Mackay, oceanographer James Murray, anthropologist Henri Beuchat and seaman Stanley Morris -- left the shipwreck camp on their own initiative in early February 1914, over Bartlett's objections and refusing his offer of a search or support party. They too had not been seen again.
The crossing from the wreck site to Wrangel Island required navigating pressure ridges up to a hundred feet high and left the surviving party exhausted, with several men injured.

No government, ship's captain or family member outside the expedition knew the Karluk's survivors had reached Wrangel Island. The ship had last been reported drifting in the ice far to the east months earlier, and expedition leader Vilhjalmur Stefansson -- who had left the ship in September 1913 before it drifted away -- had already reported it missing to Canadian officials. What the outside world believed is reconstructed from the record rather than something the party could confirm from where they stood.

Wrangel Island offered some subsistence: driftwood for fuel and shelter material, and game -- seals, polar bears, birds -- that an experienced hunter could pursue. The open sea ice offered none of this.
Bartlett's original plan, announced immediately after the sinking, had been to lead the whole party first to Wrangel Island and then onward together to the Siberian mainland.

Kataktovik, the Inupiat hunter hired at Cape Smythe, Alaska before the Karluk became trapped, was experienced in long-distance sea-ice travel and dog-sledge navigation -- unlike most of the ship's company of scientists, sailors and officers, who had little or no Arctic field experience.

Bartlett and Kataktovik would take six weeks to cross the ice and make landfall near Cape Jakan around April 4, 1914, then travel overland along the coast before reaching a whaling ship and eventually Alaska. None of that outcome was knowable when they set out.
Three more members of the party left at Wrangel Island -- Bjarne Mamen, George Malloch and George Breddy -- would die during Bartlett's roughly six-month absence, before rescue arrived.

Rescue would not come until September 7, 1914, almost eight months after the sinking, when the schooner King and Winge reached Wrangel Island and took off the 14 surviving members of the main party. An earlier relief attempt by the U.S. Revenue Cutter Bear could not reach the island through the ice.
The fate of the Mackay group would never be established. The Anderson party's remains would be found on Herald Island only in 1924.

Decades later, historians working with correspondence not publicly available at the time -- including Bartlett's private letters and the papers of expedition scientist Rudolph Anderson -- would conclude that Bartlett and Stefansson both bore significant, contested responsibility for the decisions that put the Karluk into the ice in the first place. That reassessment was available to nobody judging Bartlett's conduct in 1914.

evidence.title: Source disagreements recorded in the research record
evidence.author_or_institution: Research record for this case (see src-01 through src-07)
evidence.supported_claim: Two points are unsettled. First, why Mackay, Murray, Beuchat and Morris left in February: accounts cite resentment of Bartlett's authority, fear of the camp drifting further from land, and in at least one account drug use by Mackay. No single motive is treated here as settled, and that departure is deliberately not used as this case's decision -- it was not a two-option choice Bartlett made but an independent departure he did not authorise and only partly tried to dissuade. Second, how much responsibility Bartlett bears overall: accounts range from Jennifer Niven's heroic portrait to William R. Hunt's sharp criticism of his handling of the ship to Cavell's source-based conclusion that Bartlett and Stefansson share serious but different responsibility. This case confines itself to the narrower, well-documented decision at Wrangel Island and does not adjudicate that dispute.
